title: The Discovery of Silk
tagline: A cocoon falls into tea — and civilization is changed forever.

scenes.text: China, c. 2700 BCE. The Yellow Emperor's court sits beneath ancient mulberry trees. The Empress Lei Zu is pouring tea in the imperial garden when something extraordinary happens — a small cocoon drops from a mulberry branch into her steaming cup.

scenes.speaker: Lei Zu
scenes.text: Look — the hot water has loosened something. A thread. A single unbroken thread, fine as breath, strong as fiber. It unwinds and unwinds... How long is this thread? How can it be so long from such a small cocoon?

challenge.instruction: The thread keeps unwinding from the cocoon in Lei Zu's cup. How long is it? Add each length to the count as it comes off.
challenge.fact: Chinese tradition credits Lei Zu (also written Leizu or Si Ling-chi), wife of the Yellow Emperor Huangdi, with discovering silk around 2700 BCE when a silkworm cocoon fell into her tea and she unravelled its thread.

scenes.text: Lei Zu did not just discover silk — she mastered it. She studied the silkworm's life cycle, cultivated mulberry trees to feed them, and invented the silk loom to weave the gossamer threads into fabric. She is venerated in China as the Silkworm Mother.

scenes.speaker: Court Official
scenes.text: Empress, this fabric is like nothing we have ever worn. Lighter than linen, stronger than hemp, and it catches the light like water. The Emperor will want to know its secret kept within the kingdom.

challenge.instruction: Silkworms eat nothing but mulberry leaves. Lead water to the mulberry grove so that the palace worms never go hungry.
challenge.fact: Chinese tradition credits Lei Zu with teaching people to plant mulberries and raise silkworms as well as to reel silk. Sericulture became women's work, and empresses performed a yearly rite of gathering mulberry leaves.

scenes.speaker: Lei Zu
scenes.text: The silk road will one day carry this fabric to the ends of the world. But the secret of how to make it — the worm, the leaf, the loom — that knowledge belongs to China. Guard it carefully. An empire built on silk is an empire built on threads no army can cut.

challenge.instruction: Guard the secret carefully. Raise a rammed-earth wall around the silk-house, one tamped layer at a time.
challenge.fact: China kept sericulture to itself for thousands of years. By one legend the secret left only when a Chinese princess, married to the king of Khotan, smuggled silkworm eggs out in her headdress — a story recorded by the pilgrim Xuanzang in the 7th century.

scenes.text: For three thousand years, China kept the secret of silk-making on pain of death. Roman senators wore silk robes and had no idea where the fabric came from, calling China 'the land of Seres' — the silk people. The Silk Road that Lei Zu's discovery made possible connected every major civilization on earth.

challenge.instruction: Lei Zu's thread will one day cross the world. Lead a caravan from Chang'an to Constantinople and sell the silk where it is rarest.
challenge.fact: Silk reached Rome through many middlemen. In 14 CE the Senate forbade men to wear it, and Pliny the Elder complained that India, China and Arabia drained a hundred million sesterces a year from the empire for luxuries.

scenes.speaker: Lei Zu
scenes.text: A single silkworm produces up to 900 meters of thread in its short life. I spent my life learning to listen to small things. A cocoon in a teacup. A thread too fine to see. The greatest discoveries do not announce themselves — they wait for someone patient enough to notice.

challenge.instruction: Lei Zu learned by noticing small patterns. Restore the dots on the Luo River turtle's shell so that every line has the same sum.
challenge.fact: The Lo Shu is among the oldest magic squares known. Chinese tradition ties it to Yu the Great, the legendary tamer of floods, who is placed a few centuries after the Yellow Emperor and Lei Zu.

challenge.instruction: The greatest discoveries wait for someone patient enough to notice. Study the shape while it is shown, then build it from memory.
challenge.fact: Lei Zu's story comes from later texts, but archaeology bears out the age of Chinese silk: woven silk from about 2700 BCE has been found in Zhejiang, and traces of silk protein in tombs at Jiahu are some 8,500 years old.

scenes.speaker: Lei Zu
scenes.text: The lesson is simple. Ashurbanipal stands at Memphis and the Business War has begun. Bring me onto the board, put a Noble at my side, and let us measure Wealth against Wealth.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 1 · First Duel. Deploy Lei Zu to Memphis, add the Noble, then tap Lei Zu and tap Ashurbanipal to attack. Win one attack.
challenge.fact: In a Local Event every card at the location counts: Lei Zu brings 10 Wealth, the Noble adds +2 (or +4 beside a Great Person who shares that identity), and the higher total wins the attack. The loser returns to its owner's hand unless Kill mode is on.
